data.title: Corporate Credentials Present in Public Breach Data
data.summary: Corporate email addresses and associated passwords appeared in publicly available breach data and infostealer logs. Where staff reuse passwords, these credentials authenticate directly against corporate services.
data.description:
Breach corpora aggregate credentials from thousands of unrelated services, and infostealer logs — harvested from infected personal machines — add session cookies and saved browser passwords, often including corporate ones entered on a home device.

Credential stuffing then needs no skill: the pairs are tried against every exposed service until one works. Password reuse between a personal account and a corporate one is the mechanism, and it remains common despite instruction.

Infostealer output is the more urgent form, because it may include valid session cookies that bypass authentication altogether, including multi-factor, until the session expires or is revoked.
data.recommendation:
* Monitor breach and infostealer sources for your domains continuously, and force a reset on any match.
* Screen passwords against a breached-password corpus at the point they are set.
* Deploy phishing-resistant MFA, which limits the value of a reused password.
* Revoke sessions, not only passwords, when exposure is found — a stolen cookie survives a password change.
* Discourage corporate account use on personal devices, and provide managed alternatives that make that practical.
data.short_recommendation: Monitor breach corpora and block reused passwords.
